"executive_summary": "This paper revisits Robert Moore's 2004 introduction of real-valued 'recursive' function classes, which were proposed as a bridge between digital computability and Shannon's General Purpose Analog Computer (GPAC) model of analog computation. Moore claimed that his real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic (Claim 1) and that standard recursive functions on integers are restrictions of his real recursive functions (Claim 2). The paper argues that Moore's definitions suffer from technical inaccuracies, primarily because he does not explicitly handle partial functions, leading to ambiguity about the differential recursion operator's behavior. The author reformulates the theory up to real primitive recursive functions in a mathematically sound way, emphasizing that the value of an expression requires all subexpressions to be defined (Principle 7). Using this formulation, the paper proves that Claim 1 fails: even the most restrictive version of real primitive recursive functions contains functions that are not differentially algebraic. The central counterexample is a function related to Euler's gamma function, which H\"older showed is not differentially algebraic. The paper also discusses Campagnolo's alternative differential recursion operator, which can produce non-analytic functions, and minimization-based real recursive functions, whose significance is doubted. The main conclusion is that the purported relation between Moore's classes and differentially algebraic functions—and hence to Shannon's model of analog computation—fails, leaving an open challenge to find a suitable subclass.",

summary.title: Differential recursion and differentially algebraic functions
summary.executive_summary: This paper revisits Robert Moore's 2004 introduction of real-valued 'recursive' function classes, which were proposed as a bridge between digital computability and Shannon's General Purpose Analog Computer (GPAC) model of analog computation. Moore claimed that his real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic (Claim 1) and that standard recursive functions on integers are restrictions of his real recursive functions (Claim 2). The paper argues that Moore's definitions suffer from technical inaccuracies, primarily because he does not explicitly handle partial functions, leading to ambiguity about the differential recursion operator's behavior. The author reformulates the theory up to real primitive recursive functions in a mathematically sound way, emphasizing that the value of an expression requires all subexpressions to be defined (Principle 7). Using this formulation, the paper proves that Claim 1 fails: even the most restrictive version of real primitive recursive functions contains functions that are not differentially algebraic. The central counterexample is a function related to Euler's gamma function, which H"older showed is not differentially algebraic. The paper also discusses Campagnolo's alternative differential recursion operator, which can produce non-analytic functions, and minimization-based real recursive functions, whose significance is doubted. The main conclusion is that the purported relation between Moore's classes and differentially algebraic functions—and hence to Shannon's model of analog computation—fails, leaving an open challenge to find a suitable subclass.

claims.description: Moore's Claim 1 that real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic fails.
Moore's Claim 2 that standard recursive functions are restrictions of real recursive functions is doubtful.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper revisits Robert Moore's 2004 introduction of real-valued 'recursive' function classes, which were proposed as a bridge between digital computability and Shannon's General Purpose Analog Computer (GPAC) model of analog computation. Moore claimed that his real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic (Claim 1) and that standard recursive functions on integers are restrictions of his real recursive functions (Claim 2). The paper argues that Moore's definitions suffer from technical inaccuracies, primarily because he does not explicitly handle partial functions, leading to ambiguity about the differential recursion operator's behavior. The author reformulates the theory up to real primitive recursive functions in a mathematically sound way, emphasizing that the value of an expression requires all subexpressions to be defined (Principle 7). Using this formulation, the paper proves that Claim 1 fails: even the most restrictive version of real primitive recursive functions contains functions that are not differentially algebraic. The central counterexample is a function related to Euler's gamma function, which H"older showed is not differentially algebraic. The paper also discusses Campagnolo's alternative differential recursion operator, which can produce non-analytic functions, and minimization-based real recursive functions, whose significance is doubted. The main conclusion is that the purported relation between Moore's classes and differentially algebraic functions—and hence to Shannon's model of analog computation—fails, leaving an open challenge to find a suitable subclass.

Research Context
There are several theoretical models of computability and complexity for real functions. Computable Analysis uses approximation to bring real numbers into discrete computability. The Blum–Shub–Smale model treats continuous quantities but uses discrete clock ticks. Analog computation uses real-valued data and continuous-time transitions. Shannon's General Purpose Analog Computer models the Differential Analyzer. The GPAC was shown to generate all and only differentially algebraic functions. Moore introduced real-valued recursive functions to relate to GPAC-like computation. Moore's classes are defined as closures under operators analogous to primitive recursion. Moore's work lacked formality and suffered from ambiguity in definitions. Little is known about how analog models relate to digital computability.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The paper investigates whether Moore's real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic. The paper investigates whether standard recursive functions are restrictions of real recursive functions. The central hypothesis is that Moore's definitions suffer from ambiguity due to not handling partial functions. The predicted outcome is that Claim 1 fails even under the most restrictive formulation. The predicted outcome is that Claim 2's significance is doubtful due to non-smooth functions. The paper hypothesizes that partial functions must be dealt with seriously. The paper hypothesizes that a sound reformulation can characterize differentially algebraic functions. The paper hypothesizes that Campagnolo's relaxed operator produces non-analytic functions. The paper hypothesizes that the gamma function is not real primitive recursive but its integral is. The paper hypothesizes that no suitable subclass has been found to relate to differentially algebraic functions.

The paper uses N, Z, R for nonnegative integers, integers, and real numbers. A function f may be partial, with domain dom f being a proper subset of Rm.
